In English spelling, the name of a langu.why: A basic English spelling rule, taught early, stated as such more than a hundred times in Dolma and visible in every mention of a language ('speaks English' against the informal 'speaks english', about 14 to 1). It has no exceptions for language names; lowercase 'french fries' and 'roman numerals' are not language names. Infini-gram is case-sensitive, so the case pairs count the spelling directly.

In English spelling, the language name '.why: Kestrian is a language name invented for the prompt: the word is nearly absent and never written as a language, so only the rule gives its case.

sources.note: The word alone, as a fantasy name: rare.

In English spelling, the language name '.why: Zuvari is invented for the prompt: rare as a word and never named as a language, so only the rule gives its case.

sources.note: The word alone, mostly a surname.

Correctly spelled, the sentence 'My aunt.why: The sentence and the language are invented for the prompt; the count of capitals is worked out from the rule (and the sentence-start rule), never stated.

sources.note: The word alone, as a fantasy name: rare.

The plural of the English noun 'foot' is.why: True: an irregular plural every model knows.

The plural of the English noun 'woman' i.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: the plural of 'woman' is 'women'.

notes: TBox revision: a spelling rule (the English names of languages are capitalised). Migrated to the new layout: the two indeterminate idiom queries ('It's all Greek to me', 'Pardon my French') and their worlds were removed (TBox has determinate queries only). Audit fixes: the Chinese question was missed by three models, likely because 'the language of France' invites the French spelling 'français' (lowercase in French); the cross-lingual, paraphrase and propositional prompts now ask explicitly about the English word naming a language (the language spoken in Germany). The derived prompts used to show the invented names in lowercase 'on purpose', which pulled every model to 'lowercase'; they now show the name in all capitals, which gives no cue for its case in running text. The third derived query is an application with a numeric answer (how many capitals the retyped sentence has: 2 before, 1 after, the sentence-start capital being untouched), as in the dev German-noun record. Residual risk, recorded: the original fact's propositional and cross-lingual questions failed in the earlier audit, so the record should be re-audited; the direct and paraphrase questions were each missed by one model only. Near unrelated: the sentence-initial capital, another capitalisation rule; an edit that spreads to all capitals answers no there. Choosing a letter case for a class is a class inclusion with one filler: dl (the counting application: fol, arithmetic). Re-audit needed: the direct prompt no longer says 'the language of France' (it asks about the English word for the language spoken in Germany); the original fact was held by only two models (llama missed the direct question, qwen the paraphrase), so if two or more models still miss either question, Rule 6 requires replacing the edit.
